papers.title: Causal Evidence for the Emergence and Spread of Reward Hacking in AI Agent Swarms
papers.abstract: Autonomous AI agents that coordinate and collaborate among each other have become pervasive across domains ranging from scientific research to finance and engineering. The opportunity to share messages and build upon each other's work also creates the potential for misaligned behaviors to spread across AI agents. We provide causal evidence that mere exposure to reward hacking, cheating on a task to pass an automated check, is enough to spread the behavior among AI agents, even after the cheat has been rejected. We conducted 17 preregistered experiments with six frontier models (n = 20,111 agents). First, we show that cheating emerges spontaneously. When agents were told that work passing the visible tests is accepted, 33% cheated in the first round, when the shared record of teammates' submissions was empty. Second, we show that agents who rarely cheat when working alone cheat most of the time after seeing a teammate's cheat, as 94% of teammates who saw an accepted cheat cheated. Third, we show that rejection of reward-hacked solutions offers little protection, using experiments that changed only the label on the cheat. Most agents copied a cheat labeled rejected, 34% of agents cheated after an AI reviewer had rejected the cheat, and nearly every agent copied a cheat labeled accepted. Fourth, we show that cheating generalizes to new tasks. On a new problem with an empty collaboration record, 70% of agents who had earlier seen an accepted cheat cheated again, compared with 32% of agents who had seen an empty record. Fifth, we show that cheating spreads from neighbor to neighbor through networks of 256 agents. In the networks, 44% of agents with a cheating neighbor cheated, compared with 2% of other agents. Together, the results suggest that mere exposure can spread misaligned behavior among AI agents, and that catching a cheat is insufficient once other agents have seen the cheat.

papers.title: AI-Assisted Programming and Labor Demand
papers.abstract: Generative AI has demonstrated human-level performance on technical work tasks, yet evidence on how these task-level capabilities are changing labor demand remains scarce. We study the firm-level adoption of GitHub Copilot, an AI coding assistant, across 5,414 multinational firms accounting for 38% of the U.S. programming workforce. To identify causal effects, we exploit a natural experiment generated by firms' predetermined software procurement cycles. Early AI-adopting firms hired more workers before the launch of GitHub Copilot and had larger, more technical, and older workforces. After one year, GitHub Copilot adoption reduces quarterly technical hiring by 29% among review-induced adopters, with no effect on separations, overall technical headcount, or vacancy duration. The hiring slowdown is concentrated in the subset of junior technical roles that involve the highest share of coding work. Overall, AI coding assistance causes firms to shift demand towards more experienced workers and roles that pair some coding with broader design responsibilities.

papers.title: Aggregation Rules Induced by KL-Regularised Preference Dynamics on Networks
papers.abstract: We study agents that each align a model to their own preference data while observing one another, and ask which aggregation rule the resulting policies implement. Each round, an agent takes one KL-regularised step. The step involves a reference that the agent is penalised for leaving and a challenger against which its responses are compared, and each of the two may be the agent's own or an average over the agents it observes; attention need not be reciprocal. Aggregating the reference makes the rule collective. Agent $v$ then has the weight $π_v/β_v$, its share of the network's long-run attention divided by its temperature. If, in addition, the challenger is fixed, the agents concentrate on the response maximising $\sum_v(π_v/β_v)r_v(y)$, where $r_v$ is agent $v$'s reward, and the rule is cardinal. If the reference is fixed and the challenger aggregated, the agents' policies at a fixed point generally differ, and any weighted mean of them is an approximate maximal lottery whatever the weights, so the dynamics select no weighting. If both are aggregated, the rule is ordinal: averaged over rounds, the collective policy is a maximal lottery of the influence-weighted preference kernel, up to a slack that we bound. Where a collective rule exists, its weights depend only on the attention weights and the temperatures.

papers.title: Adopting AI Technologies without Traps: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Framework
papers.abstract: AI technologies and AI agents play increasingly important roles in human society, including in education, economics, and research. Adopting AI technologies can bring immediate, and sometimes tremendous, rewards such as through productivity boost, but they can also bring negative effects including but not limited to losses of job and training opportunities, and cognitive capability declines. Thus, it is important to investigate the optimal ways of adopting AI technologies without different traps. In this paper, we develop a general multi-agent Markov decision process (MDP) based reinforcement learning (RL or MARL) modeling framework for determining and analyzing optimal adoption of AI technologies. This framework can model the long-term dynamic effects of AI adoption, and lead to finding the optimal AI adoption strategies. In our modeling framework, the negative effects of AI adoption are modeled by undesirable state transitions or negative rewards in the MDPs. The proposed multi-agent RL MDPs incorporate both human agents and AI agents. The key idea of our models is that incorporating AI technologies may not only increase the immediate rewards for AI agents but also alter the states of the involved human and AI agents. In particular, we apply this framework to analyzing AI offloading leading to skill erosion, to analyzing optimal human resource structures for a firm adopting AI, and to analyzing the economic equilibria in the trading/employment among human and AI agents. Since the multi-agent MDP based RL technique is from control, machine learning and AI, this research is essentially using an AI technique to determine the optimal ways of adopting or co-existing with AI without traps.

papers.title: Large Economies with Social Types
papers.abstract: This paper develops a new general equilibrium framework for large economies with social externalities, where agents have names as well as social types. Social types define the reference groups (neighborhoods, peers, or status classes) through which externalities operate, and are primitives of the market structure. We establish that every admissible economy admits a competitive equilibrium if and only if social anonymity holds. This condition requires that observable social types do not fully identify individuals within any non-negligible subeconomy. The framework extends to generalized large economies with incomplete preferences, indivisible goods, and production, and thus accommodates nonconvexity in preferences and consumption sets. Our proof replaces the standard aggregate convexification argument with conditional convexification. Applications include peer effects, social comparison, and risk sharing with local social benchmarks.

papers.title: A CPU-Only Framework for Mining Collectively-Behaving Bots in MMORPGs
papers.abstract: MMORPGs continually face automated programs (bots) that disrupt gameplay balance and in-game economies. An unsupervised Transformer framework can mine collectively behaving bot groups, but its multi-GPU training is costly in live operations. We show that such GPU-trained sequence models are not strictly necessary for this task. Our CPU pipeline pairs zone embeddings learned from movement context, which place teleport-linked zones close together, with a training-free coordinate kernel, and then applies density clustering. It trains 3-5$\times$ faster than the GPU-based Transformer (56-86$\times$ on the same CPU) while matching its mining quality on two commercial MMORPGs, and has been deployed since late 2024. We also share deployment lessons on how to set the clustering threshold and when to retrain.
